cultures.name: Chinese
cultures.mythology_summary: In this Chinese Xingguan tradition, 北斗 (Běi Dǒu, Northern Dipper) is a seven-star asterism. It is not the same figure as the IAU constellation Ursa Major, though the same seven bright stars lie inside that IAU area.

entries.mythology_summary: In this Chinese Xingguan tradition, 北斗 (Běi Dǒu, Northern Dipper) is a seven-star asterism recorded in Stellarium's Chinese sky culture from the Yixiang Kaocheng tradition. Xingguan are star-official groupings without IAU-style boundaries.
entries.science_summary: The same seven stars are Dubhe, Merak, Phecda, Megrez, Alioth, Mizar, and Alkaid. In modern astronomy they form the Plough / Big Dipper asterism inside Ursa Major. Scientific names below are modern identifiers, not Chinese catalogue names.
entries.story_summary: In this Chinese Xingguan tradition, 北斗 is a northern seven-star grouping. Stellarium lists the primary stars as HIP 54061, 53910, 58001, 59774, 62956, 65378, and 67301.
entries.astronomy_context: These HIP identifiers correspond to Dubhe through Alkaid. This story does not treat the IAU Great Bear as a Chinese figure.

cultures.name: Chinese
cultures.mythology_summary: In this Chinese Xingguan tradition, 织女 and 河鼓 are two separate asterisms. They sit in the modern IAU areas of Lyra and Aquila. They are not Chinese versions of those IAU constellations.

entries.mythology_summary: In this Chinese Xingguan tradition, 织女 (Zhī Nǚ, Weaving Girl) is a three-star grouping around Vega, and 河鼓 (Hé Gǔ, Drum at the River) is the three-star line Altair–Tarazed–Alshain. Stellarium also records 牛郎 as an alternate label on 河鼓二 (Altair). Folklore associated with Qixi is a later popular layer and is not treated here as the Xingguan definition.
entries.science_summary: Vega and Altair are nearby bright A-type stars on opposite sides of the Milky Way band. Scientific NASA or Chandra media for these stars, if shown, is a modern scientific view and is not a source for the Xingguan.
entries.story_summary: Two Xingguan spanning the IAU constellations Lyra and Aquila.

entries.tradition_name: Māori astronomical tradition (Tātai Arorangi), as documented in Stellarium's Māori sky culture

cultures.name: Māori
cultures.mythology_summary: In the Māori tradition represented by this story, Matariki is the Pleiades. Stellarium's Māori pack notes iwi (tribal) variation in star naming and records Matariki as the well-known name for this cluster.

entries.mythology_summary: In the Māori tradition represented by this story, Matariki names the Pleiades. Stellarium's Māori sky culture, following published sources including Elsdon Best's Dominion Museum monographs, treats Matariki as seasonal and navigational sky knowledge. This is not a generic Polynesian story, and it is not the Greek Pleiades myth.
entries.science_summary: The Pleiades (M45) is a nearby open cluster in Taurus. NASA imagery of the cluster is a modern scientific view and is not a Māori source.
entries.story_summary: Matariki is the Māori name for the Pleiades in the Stellarium Māori pack.
entries.astronomy_context: M45 / Alcyone and neighbouring bright cluster members.

cultures.mythology_summary: In this Arabian Peninsula stellar tradition, al-Thurayyā is the Pleiades and is used in seasonal timing. Stellarium records that some local calendars begin the year with the heliacal rising of al-Thurayyā.

entries.mythology_summary: In this Arabian Peninsula stellar tradition — not medieval Islamic astronomy and not a collapsed folk category — al-Thurayyā is the Pleiades. Stellarium's Arabian Peninsula sky culture, drawing on documented poetry and anwāʾ commentary, describes star timing for travel, weather, and agriculture. Other names and legends in that pack belong to different asterisms and are not merged here.
entries.science_summary: The Pleiades are a nearby open cluster. Official NASA images of the cluster are scientific media, not the cultural source.

cultures.name: Medieval Islamic astronomy (al-Ṣūfī)
cultures.mythology_summary: In al-Ṣūfī's Book of Fixed Stars, the Lyre is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. Stellarium's arabic_al-sufi pack labels it al-Lawrā. This is a scientific treatise tradition, not Peninsula folk star lore.

entries.mythology_summary: In the medieval Islamic astronomical tradition represented by this story, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ṣūfī (903–986) described the Lyre among Ptolemy's 48 constellations in the Book of Fixed Stars, shortly before 964. Stellarium's Al-Sufi sky culture, following Paul Kunitzsch's account, presents each constellation with discussion, indigenous Arabic star-name identifications, globe/sky drawings, and a Ptolemaic table. This is not Arabian Peninsula oral tradition and is not labeled Arab mythology.
entries.science_summary: The same IAU area is Lyra, with Vega as lucida. Modern photometry and NASA imagery are later scientific views.

entries.mythology_summary: Archaeological interpretations suggest that three sandstone slabs on Fajada Butte, at Chaco Culture National Historical Park, once sent dagger-shaped midday sunlight across two spiral petroglyphs at the solstices and equinoxes. The National Park Service reports the site is no longer open; visitor erosion later shifted the slabs so the original centered summer pattern no longer occurs. This card does not claim to retell a living Pueblo oral story.

entries.mythology_summary: Archaeological interpretations suggest that Pueblo Bonito and other Chaco Canyon constructions include walls and axes within a fraction of a degree of true north–south and east–west. Knowledge of those axes can mark solar noon and the equinoxes. Polaris is shown in the tour only as a modern north-sky reference. It is not presented as an Ancestral Puebloan constellation. The popular Casa Rinconada niche-light effect is omitted because reconstruction makes the original opening uncertain.

entries.mythology_summary: In the Mexica historical sources represented here, Tianquiztli — the marketplace — is identified with the Pleiades (Spanish colonial 'Cabrillas' / 'Mastelejos'). Sahagún's Primeros Memoriales draws a compact many-star figure. Related colonial and INAH discussions connect the midnight culmination of this group to the New Fire ceremony that bound the 52-year cycle (xiuhmolpilli) at Huixachtécatl, the Hill of the Star. This is historical calendrical astronomy, not a modern Nahua teaching and not a collapsed folk category. Other Primeros Memoriales figures with conflicting star identifications are not merged here.
entries.science_summary: The Pleiades (M45) are a nearby open cluster in Taurus. Official NASA images of the cluster are a scientific view and are not a Mexica source.

entries.mythology_summary: This archaeological interpretation of Mexica observations, supported by measured building orientations and Sahagún's feast calendar, suggests that sunrise alignments from the Templo Mayor toward Mount Tlaloc and other eastern peaks helped keep an agricultural year. Šprajc documented Templo Mayor solar dates; a 2022 PNAS study reconstructs Basin sunrise observatories. This is not a constellation figure and is not merged with Maya astronomy.

entries.mythology_summary: Archaeological evidence suggests, and the National Park Service interprets, that Ancestral Puebloan observers at Hovenweep's Holly Unit marked the summer solstice on a petroglyph panel. A beam of light through a narrow gap between boulders bisects spiral and concentric-circle marks on the solstice and nearby mornings. Researchers have interpreted this as a public seasonal marker, not as a living Pueblo oral story.
entries.science_summary: At mid-northern latitudes the rising Sun reaches its northernmost azimuth near the June solstice. A fixed gap and marked rock face can record that extreme. NASA solar imagery, if shown, is a modern scientific view and is not an Ancestral Puebloan source.
